title: What is inventory?
subtitle: Asset or burden - it depends on how it's managed
openingQuestion: Inventory growing faster than revenue is a sign of what?
openingOptions: Goods may be selling slowly or piling up
explanation: Inventory is an asset on the balance sheet, but it's really cash being held hostage: already paid to the supplier and not yet collected back from a customer. That's why the key figure isn't the inventory level but how fast it turns over. Inventory growing faster than revenue is almost always a sign goods are selling slowly, and for industries like fashion or electronics, goods sitting too long also carry the risk of a forced fire sale.

realWorldExample.description: The Bach Hoa Xanh retail chain has to tightly manage its fresh-food inventory - too much leads to spoilage, too little leads to stock-outs and lost revenue, requiring a delicate balance between the two risks.

quiz.question: What are the three layers of inventory for a manufacturing business?
options: Goods in the warehouse, goods in transit, and goods already sold
Imported goods, domestic goods, and consignment goods
New goods, aged goods, and goods awaiting liquidation
Raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods
quiz.explanation: The three layers reflect three stages of the production chain: uncut fabric, a shirt still being sewn, a finished shirt ready to go. A trading business only has a single layer: goods bought to resell, with no production step.

quiz.question: Inventory rises 40% while revenue rises only 5%. What signal is this?
options: Warning: goods may be selling more slowly than expected
Positive: the business is stocking up early for a peak season
Neutral: these two indicators aren't inherently related to each other
Warning: the business is about to run short of stock to deliver to customers
quiz.explanation: When sales are good, inventory and revenue rise at the same pace. Inventory swelling much faster means either goods are selling slowly while the company still stocks according to the old plan, or the product is starting to go stale - both leading to a forced discount to clear stock.

quiz.question: Cost of goods sold is 1,200 billion, average inventory is 200 billion. What is the inventory turnover ratio?
options: 0.17 times (= 200 ÷ 1,200, flipping numerator and denominator)
6 times per year (= 1,200 ÷ 200)
1,000 billion (= 1,200 − 200, taking the difference)
12 times (= 1,200 ÷ 100, wrong inventory figure)
quiz.explanation: Inventory Turnover = COGS / Average Inventory = 1,200/200 = 6 times. Dividing 365 by 6 gives about 61 days - the average time a batch of goods sits in the warehouse before it's sold.

quiz.question: Why is inventory called tied-up capital even though it's still an asset?
options: Because inventory is subject to an annual asset tax until it's sold
Because accounting doesn't allow inventory to be recorded at market value
Because cash has already been spent but hasn't come back until the goods are sold
Because inventory isn't counted as part of a business's current assets
quiz.explanation: A batch of goods sitting idle is still an asset on the books, but it's cash spent that hasn't come back. The more capital sits in the warehouse, the less is left to pay salaries, pay suppliers, or invest.

quiz.question: What is the specific risk of fashion inventory compared to dry-food inventory?
options: Higher import tax applied to garment goods
Faster physical spoilage due to storage conditions
Higher storage costs because it needs more space
Losing value from going out of style even while physically intact
quiz.explanation: Dry food has a long shelf life; an outdated garment breaks down economically rather than physically. A season-old shirt can lose 50-70% of its value while still brand new.

keyTakeaways: Inventory is tied-up capital - it needs tight management
Inventory growing faster than revenue is a warning signal

practicePrompt.question: Retailer X has Inventory up 40% while Revenue is up only 8% compared to last year. What signal is this for investors?
options: A positive signal - the company is stocking up abundantly to get ahead of strong future demand growth
A warning - goods may be selling slower than planned, with capital stuck in the warehouse
No meaning at all, since inventory isn't related to core business performance
It simply reflects the company opening a number of new retail stores
practicePrompt.explanation: Inventory growing faster than Revenue is a classic warning signal: inventory is tied-up capital, and if it's growing faster than sales, it means goods are selling more slowly, or the company misjudged market demand.

application.title: Estimate inventory turnover for a store you know
application.message: If you or someone you know runs a business with inventory, try estimating: on average how long does it take incoming stock to sell out, and compared to a few months ago - is that speeding up or slowing down?
application.secondary: If you don't have business data to hand, watch a store you visit often to practise this way of thinking.

sections.text: Inventory sits in the current-assets group, but differs from cash in one important way: it may not turn into cash at all. A batch of goods sitting idle in a warehouse is still recorded as an 'asset' on the balance sheet, even though in reality it's dead money waiting to be sold - or worse, waiting to be liquidated at a loss.

For a manufacturing business, inventory splits into three layers: raw materials not yet put into production, work-in-progress on the production line, and finished goods ready to sell. For a trading business - retail, distribution - there's only one type: goods bought to resell, with no production step.

items: Raw materials: fabric, steel coil, raw fresh milk...
Work-in-progress: a shirt still being sewn, steel still being rolled...
Finished goods: a completed shirt, bundled steel bars ready to ship to a dealer

sections.text: Why inventory growing faster than revenue is a bad signal

When a company is selling well, inventory and revenue usually rise at the same pace - inventory turns over evenly to meet demand. But if inventory swells much faster than revenue, there are three possibilities: (1) goods are selling more slowly than expected while the company keeps producing/stocking under the old plan, (2) products are starting to go out of date or lose competitiveness, (3) the company is deliberately stockpiling to speculate on raw-material prices. Cases (1) and (2) both lead to the risk of deep discounting or an inventory write-down provision - a hidden loss not yet on the income statement but soon to be recognised.

sections.label: Metric to remember
sections.text: Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) / Average Inventory. The higher the turnover, the faster goods rotate and the less capital sits idle in the warehouse. Food retail has high turnover (10-15 times/year), while luxury goods or real estate have very low turnover (under 1 time/year) because the products' nature is completely different.

concepts.def: Current assets including raw materials, work-in-progress, and unsold finished goods
COGS / Average Inventory - measures how fast goods rotate
365 / Inventory Turnover - the average number of days goods sit in the warehouse

left.label: High Turnover
left.text: Goods rotate quickly, little capital tied up, low obsolescence risk - common in food retail, F&B

right.label: Low Turnover
right.text: Goods sit for a long time, a lot of capital tied up, high risk of markdown or obsolescence - common in luxury goods, industrial machinery

lines: Inventory is a conditional asset - it's only really valuable once it sells at a good price.
Tracking inventory growth against revenue is the earliest way to spot a sales problem.
Inventory Turnover and DIO are two indicators you must check when analysing any business with physical goods.
